newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - British spin doctors run campaign with iron rod.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - British spin doctors run campaign with iron rod.

text.p: Lights, music, action. Another slick Labour news conference gets underway in the party's futuristic media centre, and all under the miss-nothing gaze of spin-doctor-in-chief Peter Mandelson.
Mandelson has revolutionised the opposition party's standing in the British media since it lost the 1992 election, and Labour is strong favourite to win the May 1 poll.
Nicknamed Svengali and Rasputin, the television producer turned member of parliament courts, cajoles and bullies Britain's media into providing the coverage he wants.
Former Labour leader Neil Kinnock, referring to critics' assessment of Mandelson as an "evil genius", is quoted as saying: "They got it half right."
Spin doctors originated in the United States but are now an integral part of political and corporate life in Britain.

The first U.S.-style spin doctor on the British political scene was Bernard Ingham, former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher's bulldog-like press secretary. Critics said Ingham believed he knew the Iron Lady so well that he used to make government policy on the hoof, leaving the cabinet to catch up.

Ingham brow-beat errant journalists into submission and even banned some newspapers from the lobby system -- off-the-record briefings that government spokesmen give to political journalists twice a day.
LEARNING FROM THE AMERICANS
Labour has learnt its skills from close study of U.S. President Bill Clinton's electioneering style, swapping expertise and staff.

For years, Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives have enjoyed the support of the bulk of Britain's newspapers, enjoying access to an "inner circle" of political correspondents known to be sympathetic to the ruling party.

But cracks have started to show, partly because of Labour's new street-wise operation. The Conservatives have suffered a series of dramatic reversals, not least the resignation of their communications boss Hugh Colver last year.
Charles Lewington, an ex-Times journalist, has filled Colver's shoes at Conservative Central Office and adopted similar "carrot and stick" tactics to those refined by Labour.

But six weeks before election, the Conservatives were dealt a huge blow by Britain's biggest-selling newspaper, The Sun, which claimed to have swung the 1992 election Major's way. The Sun declared its support for Labour leader Tony Blair.
The Sun's declaration was seen as a victory for Labour's spin doctors and a testament to the importance to a modern British election campaign of influencing the media.
The modern spin doctor knows that each member of the ever-growing press pack is desperate for an exclusive. A quiet word in the right ear can ensure a story gets splashed across the front pages.
But woe betide the journalist who strays from the agreed line. An unfavourable piece risks the full wrath of Labour's media team -- no laughing matter.

Simon Hoggart, political correspondent of the Guardian newspaper, wrote in a recent book that being the object of Mandelson's affection must be like "being gummed by a toothless Rottweiler." And that is if he likes you.
"If he doesn't, he regards you with loathing and contempt. Those who offend him are boycotted, though usually for a set period of time," Hoggart said.
LABOUR'S POLITICAL MACHINE
With Labour hot favourites to take power, few journalists can afford to alienate the Labour machine -- and Mandelson knows it.

Watching Labour's nowadays provides a stark contrast with the dark days of the early 1980s when then-Labour leader Michael Foot shambled around in a scruffy raincoat, looking like an ineffectual old man compared with the dynamic Thatcher.
A Labour news conference is orchestrated down to the last detail to provide the right pictures for television, the right soundbites for the papers and to slap down or sideline awkward questions.
Behind Mandelson is another key figure, Alastair Campbell, Labour leader Tony Blair's press secretary and right-hand man.
If Labour wins the imposing teetotaller, will almost certainly fill Ingham's old role. Campbell is no shrinking violet and as a former political journalist has unrivalled knowledge of Fleet Street.

During the 1995 Labour party conference, Campbell is credited with persuading the BBC to lead its main evening news with Blair's speech rather than the verdict in the O.J. Simpson murder trial, just breaking in the United States.
The BBC led on Blair while ITN, its commercial rival, went with Simpson. "They push and push and push and push," Michael Brunson, ITN political editor, said of the spin doctors.
Of course, there is much more to Labour's operation than the relations Mandelson and Campbell have with the press.
In its towering Millbank headquarters, overlooking London's River Thames and just along from parliament, Labour's media unit is constantly poised to react to the Conservatives.
At its heart is Excalibur, a computer database which holds information on anything political -- policy announcements, speeches, or parliamentary debate, stretching back for decades.

Labour's use of Excalibur was seen when the Conservatives unveiled a poster accusing Labour of planning 30 billion pounds ($48.5 billion) of extra public spending. Chief Treasury Secretary William Waldegrave listed what he said were 89 Labour spending pledges.

As reporters left Conservative Central Office at the end of the news conference shortly afterwards, Labour representatives were waiting with detailed rebuttals of each point. ($ = 0.618 British Pounds)
